title: Distant trans-Neptunian objects found after mid-2018 (21 orbits, a > 230 au, q > 30 au) do not show the perihelion clustering of the 2019 Planet Nine sample under the tracer survey-bias model
abstract: Question: Does the clustering in longitude of perihelion (varpi) of the most distant trans-Neptunian objects, which Brown & Batygin (2019) found for 14 objects with a > 230 au and q > 30 au, continue in objects found after their sample? Method: We used the Minor Planet Center lists of 2026-11-12 and archived lists of June/July 2018 (exactly 14 objects pass the cut in 2018). We implemented the tracer survey-bias method of Brown (2017): every MPC discovery marks a survey that could find any brighter object at the same position. We calculated bias distributions for each object from 3 million siblings and compared the observed mean canonical vectors with 100,000 bias-only sets, and we fitted a bias-weighted von Mises model. Results: The method reproduces the 2019 result (mean direction 73 deg; p = 0.054 with 2018 tracers, 0.023 with 2026 tracers; reported 0.04). The 21 new multi-opposition objects (2013 to 2025 discoveries, 10 from DECam) have a mean direction of 346 deg, near the bias direction, and p = 0.70 (2026 tracers) or 0.91 (2018 tracers). At the 2019 mean direction their concentration is kappa < 0.75 (95 %), against kappa = 1.15 (68 %: 0.6-1.6) for the 2019 sample. If the 2019 best fit were true, a likelihood as low as that of the new objects would occur in at most 0.25 % of simulated samples; the Bayes factor with the 2019 posterior as prior is about 0.18. The result holds for a > 250 au, q > 37 au, q > 42 au with i < 40 deg, non-DECam objects and six tracer-model variants. All 35 objects together give p = 0.11 for varpi. One-opposition Rubin objects of 2025-2026 with a > 150 au cluster near varpi = 270 deg because of the survey footprint; the two such MPC orbits that now have more oppositions fell to a = 42-47 au. Limitations: the tracer method is not a full survey simulator; our pole test is not calibrated against the original code; the test is phenomenological, not a specific Planet Nine model; a weaker clustering (kappa below about 0.75) is still permitted.

display.caption: Bias test of Brown & Batygin (2019). Grey: mean canonical varpi vectors of bias-only sets (uniform intrinsic angles, tracer bias model). Star: observed mean. Left and middle: the 14 objects of the 2019 sample with 2018 and 2026 tracers. Right: the 21 multi-opposition objects with a > 230 au and q > 30 au that were not in the 2019 sample. The ellipse passes through the observed point; p is the fraction of bias-only sets outside it.

Bias-weighted log-likelihood of the von Mises concentration kappa at the mean direction of the 2019 sample, relative to uniform angles. The new objects disfavour the 2019 best fit (dashed vertical line).

Left: longitude of perihelion (angle) and semimajor axis (radius, log scale) of objects with q > 30 au. Red: 2019 sample; blue squares: new objects; grey circles: one-opposition 2025-2026 orbits from JPL SBDB (not used in tests). Right: discovery longitudes of tracer TNOs before 2018-07, from 2018-07 to 2024, and Rubin discoveries of 2025-2026.

citations.reason: Brown & Batygin (2019): the clustering claim, sample definition and test statistic that we reproduce and test with new objects.
Brown & Batygin (2021): q > 42 au, i < 40 deg sample selection that we also test.
Napier et al. (2021): no clustering with survey simulators; our out-of-sample result agrees.
Bernardinelli et al. (2022): DES six-year search, source of many new objects.
Second-opposition recoveries of LSST TNOs show that one-opposition large-a orbits are unreliable; our MPC snapshot check agrees.
